title: The Virgin's smile (1883)
hookLine: a statue of Mary smiles at a frightened, sick girl and she is healed; then, strangely, she fears she lied
tomorrow: what word does Thérèse find for her first communion?

cards: Some good things are so strange you'd rather not tell anyone, in case saying it out loud ruins it. Thérèse had one.
Sick and frightened, at times not seeming to know her own sisters, she turned with them toward a statue of Mary in the room. The statue, she writes, became beautiful. It smiled at her.
And her pain vanished. Now the odd part. Right after that joy, she starts to worry that she lied.

teach.h: SHE BEGS HER MOTHER IN HEAVEN.
teach.b: Start with the prayer. Her sisters knelt and begged Mary to heal her. Thérèse, finding no help on earth, she says, turned to her Mother in heaven.
Notice where she looks: toward the statue, but the one she begs is Mary herself. Then the face.
It became so beautiful, she writes, that she had never seen anything like it, full of kindness and tenderness. But what reached the very bottom of her soul was the smile.
All her pain vanished, and quiet tears of joy ran down her cheeks. The Blessed Virgin smiled at me, she thought, how happy I am. Now the puzzle.
She decided to tell no one, or her happiness would disappear. Her sister Marie guessed, and asked, and Thérèse told her.
Later, when the nuns at Carmel questioned her about it, she began to fear she had exaggerated, even lied, and that worry stayed with her a long while.
One way to read it: a gift you can't prove feels fragile once people start picking at it. And here's one to tell a friend: the Church never requires anyone to believe a private experience like this.
Thérèse simply tells what she saw, and leaves her doubt on the page too.

how: Catholics honor images of Mary in homes and churches and ask her to pray for them; the honor is given to the person the image shows, not to the image itself.

games.q: something strange and good happened to your friend at her grandmother's funeral. people keep questioning her, and she's starting to doubt herself. what fits Thérèse's story?
o: tell it simply as what she experienced; nobody has to be made to believe it.
prove it with details, or admit she must have imagined it.
never mention it again, since telling only ruins it.
games.why: Thérèse was questioned and feared she'd lied. the Church doesn't require belief in private experiences; she told what she saw, doubt and all.

practice: If there's an image of Mary near you, a statue, a holy card, a picture on your phone, let your eyes rest on her face; if not, bring one to mind.
If you pray, you can say the angel's greeting from Luke: Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee.

wordCard.voice: The Virgin's smile. In Thérèse's telling, the moment a statue of Mary smiled at a frightened child, and her illness left her.

orig.note: the angel's greeting in Luke's Greek: 'hail, full of grace' in the Douay-Rheims.

carryVoice: Your line: she smiled. One look of kindness reached the bottom of a frightened soul. Rest well tonight.
